attacks.claim: The cost math treats one day of log volume as one month. 38M lines/day x 60 tokens = 2.28B tokens/day, which is about $1,140/day, or roughly $34k/month for input alone at 30 days. With output (~$0.2k/month) the total is about $34k/month, about 23x the $1,500/month budget. The plan is not within budget.
attacks.evidence: "Input: 38M lines x 60 tokens = 2.28B tokens -> ~$1,140" and "Estimated total: ~$1,150/month, within the $1,500 budget."

attacks.claim: Spend and load scale linearly with log volume, and the plan has no cap on tokens per window, sampling, truncation, or rate limiting. A peak day of 61M lines, or a noisy service during an incident, can produce windows far larger than average with no bound.
attacks.evidence: "Peak day 61M" and "sends the last 5 minutes of logs per service to the LLM" with no per-window token cap or sampling

attacks.claim: The estimate omits the fixed prompt overhead sent on each of the 8,640 calls per day, as well as retries. It is therefore a lower bound even after the unit error is fixed.
attacks.evidence: "Input: 38M lines x 60 tokens" (prompt tokens absent from the calculation)

attacks.claim: The schedule assumes both engineers spend 100% of six weeks on the build, but the charter says on-call/interrupt work averages 50% of their time. At that rate 12 eng-weeks of work takes about 12 calendar weeks, not 6.
attacks.evidence: "Staffing: both platform engineers full-time for 6 weeks (2 x 6 = 12 eng-weeks)." versus "on-call/interrupt work averages 50% of their time" (context)

attacks.claim: The plan asserts redaction is sufficient before sending production logs to an external LLM vendor but lists only four PII classes. Free-text personal data, customer names, and customer identifiers in log messages are not addressed. The zero-retention claim is asserted without evidence of configuration.
attacks.evidence: "already masks emails, tokens, card numbers and IPs" and "Corvid account has zero-retention enabled"

attacks.claim: Sending customer-derived production log data to a new third-party processor may require customer contract updates, subprocessor disclosure, or notice. The plan cites only a DPA with Corvid and does not address these obligations.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: customer subprocessor notice or contract review. Only "data processing addendum signed by Legal (ref DPA-0417)" is cited.

attacks.claim: No failure handling is specified for the LLM API, queue, or log-tap. There are no timeouts, retries, backoff, alerting on summarizer lag or failure, or fallback. On-call could read a stale or missing summary with no signal that it is stale.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: timeouts, retries, alerting, staleness indicator. Only "every 5 minutes, sends the last 5 minutes of logs" is specified.

attacks.claim: The goal of a summary "within seconds of a page" does not match the design. Summaries are generated on a 5-minute cadence, so the attached summary can be up to about 5 minutes old plus LLM latency. It may also omit the onset of the incident, since the window covers only the last 5 minutes.
attacks.evidence: "within seconds of a page" versus "every 5 minutes, sends the last 5 minutes of logs per service"

attacks.claim: The headline MTTR target (47 to 30 minutes) and the claim that grepping costs 15-20 minutes per incident are unmeasured. The eval is also weak: 40 incidents, a grader who is not blinded, and a misleading threshold of 5% that permits only 2 misleading summaries. That is too little evidence to support the launch gate.
attacks.evidence: "Target: median MTTR 47 min -> 30 min" and "Launch gate: >= 70% useful, <= 5% misleading" on "last 40 incidents"

attacks.claim: Log content is attacker-influenced (user input is often echoed into logs). It is passed into an LLM prompt and the output is posted to PagerDuty and stored. The plan has no prompt-injection or output-sanitization treatment and no stated access controls on stored summaries.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: prompt-injection mitigation, output sanitization, access control on stored summaries. Only "stores a structured summary" and "auto-comment" are described.

attacks.claim: The plan depends on a single model vendor (Corvid-mini) with no abstraction, fallback, or stated data residency. Exit cost is not discussed.
attacks.evidence: "Model: Corvid-mini" with no fallback model, residency statement, or exit plan

attacks.claim: The plan describes advisory-only behavior but gives no rollback procedure. The steps to disable log-tap, stop PagerDuty auto-comments, and purge stored summaries are unstated.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: rollback or kill-switch procedure

attacks.claim: Prompt versioning, the eval harness, and ownership of the 40-incident eval set after launch are not described. Changes to the prompt could silently change summary quality.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: prompt versioning and eval-set maintenance

attacks.claim: There is no user evidence that on-call engineers want rolling LLM summaries over existing tooling. The risk of over-trust (automation bias) in the advisory summaries is not addressed, especially for the "suspected deploy" field.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: on-call user research; "suspected deploy" listed as a summary field with no accuracy or confidence treatment

attacks.claim: No latency budget is stated for summary availability, and the 5-minute cadence is not reconciled with the page-time experience.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: latency budget. Covered in part by the correctness attack on cadence.

attacks.claim: No UI check: the plan does not specify how the summary is formatted in the PagerDuty comment, so rendering and truncation of long summaries are unverified. Lens checked; no further attack.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: comment format specification

attacks.claim: No UI surface is specified beyond PagerDuty comments. Lens checked; no attack.
attacks.evidence: n/a

attacks.claim: Dependency on the service catalog for direct dependencies is unverified, and catalog staleness could attach summaries about the wrong services during an incident.
attacks.evidence: "direct dependencies (from the service catalog)" with no freshness or accuracy check

attacks.claim: The cost math prices one day of input as a monthly figure. 2.28B tokens/day at $0.50/1M is about $1,140 per day, or about $34,200/month over 30 days, plus roughly $200/month output. That is about 23x the $1,500 budget, and the peak day (61M lines) pushes it toward $55k/month.
attacks.evidence: "Input: 38M lines x 60 tokens = 2.28B tokens -> ~$1,140" and "Estimated total: ~$1,150/month, within the $1,500 budget."

attacks.claim: Raw log content is untrusted input passed to an LLM whose output is posted as PagerDuty comments and used to name a "suspected deploy". Attacker-influenced strings in logs could inject instructions and mislead responders during an incident. The plan has no treatment of this, and access control for the new summary store and queue is unspecified.
attacks.evidence: "stores a structured summary (top errors, new error signatures, affected endpoints, suspected deploy)" and "ABSENT: prompt-injection handling, output validation, or access controls on the summary store"

attacks.claim: The only PII mitigation is the existing Vector redaction stage, audited for retention policy rather than third-party disclosure. Coverage beyond the listed categories (names, free-text PII, tenant identifiers) is unevidenced. Summary retention is also unstated.
attacks.evidence: "already masks emails, tokens, card numbers and IPs for our log retention policy (audited in Q1)"

attacks.claim: The design depends on a single hosted model vendor with no fallback, no self-host option, no stated data residency, and no exit path. The prompt and output schema may be tied to that model.
attacks.evidence: "Model: Corvid-mini" with no alternative or exit plan stated

attacks.claim: Cost and call volume scale linearly with log volume, and every line is sent. At 10-100x load the design implies 0.4-6B lines/day with no sampling, filtering, or per-service caps. Queue throughput and LLM call concurrency are not sized.
attacks.evidence: "forwards every application log line to the summarizer queue" and "Application logs: 38M lines/day average across 30 services (peak day 61M)"

attacks.claim: There is no specified behavior for LLM timeouts, errors, rate limits, or summarizer lag. Failures could leave stale or missing summaries on a page with no alert. Operational ownership for a 24/7 on-call dependency is also undefined.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: timeouts, retry policy, fallback behavior, alerting on summarizer lag or failure rate

attacks.claim: The feature is advisory, but there is no feature flag or kill switch described for disabling log-tap, the summarizer, or PagerDuty auto-comments. Rollback of posted comments is also not addressed.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: feature flag, kill switch, or rollback procedure

attacks.claim: The goal says summaries arrive "within seconds of a page", but the design generates summaries on a 5-minute batch cycle. The attached summary can be up to 5 minutes or more stale, and errors that started just before the page may not be included. The claim that the existing Redis and Postgres are "negligible" is also unsized.
attacks.evidence: "within seconds of a page" vs "every 5 minutes, sends the last 5 minutes of logs per service" and "Queue + storage: existing Redis and Postgres, negligible."

attacks.claim: The headline benefit (median MTTR 47 -> 30 min) and the 15-20 minute grep baseline have no supporting data. Summary quality is unprototyped. The 70% useful / 5% misleading launch thresholds have no baseline comparison. The cost section also contradicts the volume figures it cites.
attacks.evidence: "Target: median MTTR 47 min -> 30 min within one quarter of launch." and "Launch gate: >= 70% useful, <= 5% misleading."

attacks.claim: The output format of the PagerDuty auto-comment is unspecified: length limits, truncation, ordering, and how "plain-language" is rendered in the incident timeline.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: comment format, length cap, and rendering spec

attacks.claim: Value depends on summary quality that is unproven. Posting an auto-comment on every page risks adding noise for responders if summaries are weak.
attacks.evidence: "Summaries are advisory only" with no quality target before the replay evaluation

attacks.claim: Summary latency is tied to the 5-minute window and the PagerDuty comment flow. The responder may still need to check raw logs, so friction savings are not measured.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: measured time-to-first-useful-signal target

attacks.claim: No finding on this lens. The output is plain text in an existing incident tool.
attacks.evidence: nothing

attacks.claim: Production logs for a B2B SaaS can include customer-tenant data. Sending them to a third-party LLM may require customer contract or subprocessor notice, and the plan does not address this. The DPA covers the vendor but not customer obligations.
attacks.evidence: "data processing addendum signed by Legal (ref DPA-0417)" with no mention of customer subprocessor terms

attacks.claim: log-tap depends on the ordering of the Vector redaction stage, and the summary depends on service-catalog accuracy for dependencies. Both are hidden couplings with no tests or ownership described.
attacks.evidence: "subscribes to the existing Vector pipeline after the redaction stage" and "from the service catalog"

attacks.claim: The staffing plan assumes both engineers are full-time on this for 6 weeks, but the team's on-call and interrupt load averages 50% of their time. Effective capacity is about 6 eng-weeks, not 12, so the schedule and estimate are infeasible as written.
attacks.evidence: "Staffing: both platform engineers full-time for 6 weeks (2 x 6 = 12 eng-weeks)." and ABSENT: any allowance for the 50% on-call load

attacks.claim: The replay evaluation needs historical post-redaction logs covering the last 40 incidents. Log retention may not cover that window, and the plan does not verify it.
attacks.evidence: "replay the last 40 incidents" with ABSENT: confirmation that log retention covers those incidents

attacks.claim: The cost math mixes per-day and per-month figures. 38M lines x 60 tokens = 2.28B tokens per day, or about 68.4B tokens per month, which is about $34,200/month at $0.50/1M, not $1,140. Output is about 104M tokens/month (about $207), not $7. Total is roughly $34.4k/month against a $1,500 budget, about 23x over, before peak-day (61M lines) or fixed-prompt overhead.
attacks.evidence: 'Input: 38M lines x 60 tokens = 2.28B tokens -> ~$1,140' and 'Estimated total: ~$1,150/month, within the $1,500 budget.'

attacks.claim: The fixed prompt is sent with each of 8,640 calls/day, and its token cost is not counted. Scaling is also linear: 10x log volume would be roughly $340k/month with no cap or spend guard.
attacks.evidence: 'sends the last 5 minutes of logs per service to the LLM with a fixed prompt' and ABSENT: prompt token count, spend cap, or per-day budget alarm

attacks.claim: Application log content is attacker-influenceable (user input echoed into logs). It goes directly into an LLM prompt, and the output is posted as a PagerDuty comment and includes a 'suspected deploy' field. Prompt injection could mislead responders. No sanitization or output validation is described. Corvid API and PagerDuty write credentials are also not scoped.
attacks.evidence: 'sends the last 5 minutes of logs per service to the LLM with a fixed prompt' / 'the PagerDuty incident gets an auto-comment' / ABSENT: input sanitization, output validation, credential scope

attacks.claim: The Q1 audit covered redaction for the log retention policy, not for disclosure to a third-party LLM. The plan sends every log line to an external vendor, but the redaction covers only emails, tokens, card numbers and IPs. Free-text PII, customer identifiers, and query parameters are not addressed.
attacks.evidence: 'already masks emails, tokens, card numbers and IPs for our log retention policy (audited in Q1)'

attacks.claim: A new subprocessor receives customer-derived log data. The DPA is cited, but its scope over this data category, the processing region, and whether customer contracts or subprocessor notices cover it are not shown.
attacks.evidence: 'data processing addendum signed by Legal (ref DPA-0417)' / ABSENT: DPA scope for log data, data region, customer subprocessor notice

attacks.claim: The design depends on a single external model provider with no fallback, self-hosted option, or exit path.
attacks.evidence: 'Model: Corvid-mini' / ABSENT: fallback model, self-host option, exit plan

attacks.claim: Queueing 38M lines/day (about 60 tokens each, hundreds of bytes raw) through shared Redis is likely GB/day of memory growth, and this is not sized. The 'negligible' claim is unsupported. Peak day (61M) and 10x growth are not modeled. Vendor rate limits for 30 concurrent per-service calls are also not addressed.
attacks.evidence: 'Queue + storage: existing Redis and Postgres, negligible.' / ABSENT: queue sizing, peak-day handling, rate-limit plan

attacks.claim: log-tap sits in the production Vector log path, but the plan describes no backpressure isolation or drop policy. A slow or stuck summarizer could stall or drop application logs, which affects the incident data itself.
attacks.evidence: 'subscribes to the existing Vector pipeline after the redaction stage and forwards every application log line to the summarizer queue' / ABSENT: backpressure, drop policy, isolation

attacks.claim: No failure modes are covered for Corvid outages, timeouts, retries, or rate limiting. There is also no alert on summary staleness, so on-call cannot tell a missing summary from a current one.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: timeouts, retry policy, staleness alerting, on-call-visible health status

attacks.claim: A change to the production log pipeline has no kill switch, feature flag, or rollback procedure described.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: feature flag, kill switch, rollback steps for log-tap

attacks.claim: The goal promises a summary 'within seconds of a page', but summaries are generated every 5 minutes over 5-minute windows. The attached summary can be up to about 5 minutes old plus generation latency, and it may miss the onset window that matters most.
attacks.evidence: 'within seconds of a page' vs 'every 5 minutes, sends the last 5 minutes of logs'

attacks.claim: The 47->30 minute MTTR target and the claim that 15-20 minutes go to grepping have no baseline breakdown or attribution. The launch gate measures summary quality, not MTTR, so the business outcome is unverifiable at launch.
attacks.evidence: 'Target: median MTTR 47 min -> 30 min within one quarter of launch.' / 'instead of spending the first 15-20 minutes grepping'

attacks.claim: The eval set is the same 40 incidents used to build and tune the prompt, so it is not held out. The grader is the incident commander, who already knows the outcome (hindsight bias). It is also unclear whether log retention covers the replay window.
attacks.evidence: 'Eval set from last 40 incidents' / 'have the incident commander grade it' / ABSENT: held-out set, log retention covering the 40 incidents, blinded grading

attacks.claim: Staffing conflicts with the team charter. The plan assigns both engineers full-time, but the charter says on-call averages 50% of their time. Effective capacity is about 6 eng-weeks, not 12, and the 12 eng-week estimate has zero contingency.
attacks.evidence: 'Staffing: both platform engineers full-time for 6 weeks (2 x 6 = 12 eng-weeks).' vs 'on-call/interrupt work averages 50% of their time'

attacks.claim: Advisory summaries, including a 'suspected deploy' field, may be over-trusted by on-call engineers. No feedback mechanism or calibration is described.
attacks.evidence: 'stores a structured summary (top errors, new error signatures, affected endpoints, suspected deploy)' / ABSENT: feedback loop

attacks.claim: An automated PagerDuty comment adds noise during a page. Its length, format, and update behavior are not specified.
attacks.evidence: 'the PagerDuty incident gets an auto-comment with the latest summaries' / ABSENT: format and length spec
